claims.text: Incorporating a minor fraction of a self-lubricating nano-additive into CoCrFeNi will trigger in-situ formation of a stable, adaptive lubricious tribofilm during sliding.
The additive-induced tribofilm will reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate from room temperature to 800 °C.
The starting CoCrFeNi matrix has a native grain structure that is likely coarse or partially refined.
The intervention is a controlled minor addition of a self-lubricating nano-additive directly into the alloy matrix.
The nano-additive will catalyze formation of a continuous lubricious film at the sliding interface.
The nano-additive may promote dynamic grain refinement of the sliding surface.
Grain refinement could modify the surface microstructure in a way favorable to wear resistance.
Sliding tribochemically activates the additive to produce an in-situ lubricious film.
The lubricious film lowers shear strength at the contact interface.
The additive-derived film mitigates oxidation damage.
Oxidation and mixed metal-oxide surface films can materially affect deformation and wear resistance in HEAs.
Self-lubricating HEA-derived nanoflakes can exhibit low friction and wear through stress-induced tribocatalytic activity under ambient sliding.
Relative to untreated CoCrFeNi, the modified alloy will have lower and more stable friction and reduced wear across 25–800 °C.
Untreated CoCrFeNi tends to show increased friction and wear under sliding, especially when oxidation and surface degradation occur.
The intervention will remain effective from 25 °C to 800 °C under loads typical of tribological testing.
Greater environmental corrosivity or temperatures above 800 °C may reduce film stability and tribological performance.
Specific wear rate can be determined from measured wear volume, normal force, and sliding distance.
Failure to achieve statistically significant decreases in both friction and wear across the tested range, or failure to form the anticipated tribofilm, will falsify the hypothesis.
